## Research motivation

I grew up in China and Singapore during a period of rapid infrastructure development. In China, I witnessed the expansion of the high-speed railway network, while in Singapore, I saw new MRT lines being built and opened throughout my childhood and teenage years. Growing up alongside these developments made me interested in how transport infrastructure transforms the connections between cities, regions, and communities.

When I started learning more about French economic history, I became interested in the development of its railway network. During the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, France built an extensive railway system connecting many cities, towns, and rural communities. As transport technologies and economic conditions changed, a substantial part of the network was eventually closed or withdrawn from passenger service.

This made me wonder what might happen to these rapidly expanding transport networks in the future. Will China and other countries eventually face challenges similar to those experienced by France? Can we learn from the historical experiences of developed countries to better anticipate and manage such changes?

These questions motivated my master's thesis on the political consequences of railway station closures in France. More broadly, I am interested in how changes in connectivity affect the distribution of economic opportunities, where people live, their employment opportunities, and inequalities between places.
